author: Trey Felton
title: Six Flags, Two Kingdoms, One Frontier - NewsBreak
text:
By Trey Felton ,
7 hours ago The Alamo is one of the most longstanding and endearing symbols of Texas. A few months back, while in San Antonio for the statewide Ben E. Keith Food Show at the gargantuan Gonzalez Convention Center on the River Walk, we walked a few blocks to visit the remarkably well-kept site known as the heart of the Texas Revolution. There, I saw a quote from a name I recognized, from 1762—over half a century before the Revolution.
Fray Mariano Francisco de los Dolores was perhaps the real impetus behind the expansion of the Spanish missions up through the Brazos River Valley, which culminated in the building of the San Xavier Mission Complex right here in Milam County. You might not know that it sat just north of Thorndale; yes, almost 300 years ago, there were three Spanish missions built at roughly the same time as the Alamo, right in our backyard. Beginning near present-day Apache Pass, they extended eastward down the path of FM 908 to near Brushy Creek, with three mission sites and a presidio.
Backyard, literally, for me—as a large portion of this land would eventually be purchased by my great-greatgrandfather Frank Worley in the early 1900s. And though he had seven kids, much of his original farmland remains with family descendants today.
The primary mission site was named for the incoming viceroy of New Spain, Juan Francisco de Güemes y Horcasitas, who governed out of Havana. It was that government that commissioned the work of Fray Mariano, in conjunction with papal edicts from Rome to spread the Gospel. Work on Mission San Xavier de las Horcasitas began in 1746, around the same time as the original Alamo in San Antonio (1744). The exact locations of the missions in Milam County were rediscovered in the 1970s by Dr. Kathleen Gilmore, 230 years they were abandoned.
The missions were only in operation a short time before they were shuttered and reestablished farther south near New Braunfels. The name San Xavier was the original name of the San Gabriel River by the earliest European explorers. At some point, a map of the area was mistranslated from San Xavier as the San Javriel River, and then again mistranslated, until it became known as the San Gabriel River.
The same thing happened to my German ancestors, who were originally the Rubecks in Germany, but when they ar- governed secularly by man and spiritually by the Word. It is mentioned by Christ with statements as simple as, “Render unto Caesar the things which are Caesar’s, and unto God the things which are God’s.”
During Jesus’ time—the bridge between the Old and New Covenant—there existed an austere overarching government in the Roman Empire and a class of spiritual leaders consisting of Pharisees, Sadducees, Zealots, and Essenes: some who wanted war with the Romans, others who wanted to coexist, and others who wanted total isolation. It’s fascinating to me that these elements persist so clearly today at the intersection of politics and religion, but I don’t have space to elaborate. I promise we’ll do that another time.
In short, Jesus shatters many of the myths and mistruths of these spiritual leaders while commanding conformity to earthly leadership which the Lord endows, and He leaves instruction on how to navigate both kingdoms.
The two-kingdoms concept was further alluded to in the sixth century by St. Augustine in City of God, and throughout the Middle Ages the power struggle between church and crown would ebb and flow. The church sought influence over the government, and vice versa. In the sixteenth century, this came to another boiling point, starting within the church and spilling over into the political realm.
One of Martin Luther’s complaints was the issue of indulgences. If the church didn’t get its way, it would cut off communion with the territory in question, thereby creating an uprising among church members. They would sell indulgences so people could still attend Mass, having been convinced this was the only way to be saved. Aside from veering into civil government matters, this offended the doctrinal ecclesiology of men like Luther and gave rise to the Protestant Reformation.
Martin Luther would articulate these grievances, as well as the doctrine of two kingdoms, in the Augsburg Confession. While Luther was already excommunicated by the Pope, his underlings partook in the Diet of Augsburg. This was an attempt to bring the churches into alignment— with each other and with the government. Again, the goal of reformers like Luther was to get back to preaching the Gospel, but the goal of Charles V was to align his forces to protect his territory from the approaching threat rived in Galveston, the name got changed to Rodenbeck— and that’s what they remain today. Once, while stationed in Germany, I took a picture next to a town called Rodenbach, just outside of Kaiserslautern, and sent it to my grandma, proclaiming this must be where our ancestors hailed from. “Nope,” she replied, before informing me that we were not known as Rodenbeck back then. I tried.
The missions left little behind, and their mysterious past gave rise to a few ghost stories—namely, the Ghost of Snively, who haunts the San Gabriel River bottoms and appears as a floating lantern at night. Snively was reputedly a treasure hunter, looking for the lost treasure of the Horcasitas mission, which was buried in a well atop the hill when the mission was overrun by the Apache.
That’s all speculation. Personally, I find it hard to believe there would be any great treasure of gold or silver sent to the frontier outpost. By most historical accounts I’ve come across, the shuttering of the missions was due partially to an extreme drought and more directly to scandal within the mission itself. It seems the presidio (military) commander was caught committing offenses by the Catholic priests, and rather than face the charges, he murdered— or conspired to murder— one of the priests, leading to a collapse in leadership across the already struggling outposts.
This seems more likely, at least to me, and despite spending hundreds of nights along the San Gabriel, I’ve never seen a floating lantern or stumbled upon gold bricks.
But why were the missions here, anyway? Ultimately, we look at the goal of the missions as converting the natives to Christianity— and it was—but there was also an intersecting goal of the Spanish government: to recruit citizens (Native Americans) to hold onto the territory from other nations prying for claim in the New World.
This is a dynamic that goes back thousands of years if you study society and governments, but I trace it back to the Israelites’ demand for a king. God warned them they would regret this, and yet they persisted, culminating with Saul, and soon after with King David, then Solomon. This created the “two kingdoms” construct: a world of the Ottomans.
Augsburg seemed to end in failure and ultimately brought religious wars throughout Europe for decades. But the principles laid out by the reformers in the Augsburg Confession continue to this day. In fact, our own Founding Father James Madison would use Luther’s writings as a basis for the separation of church and state in America.
While Article XVI is one of many in the Augsburg Confession, it is actually one of the shortest and least contentious in principle. However, in practice, the contention persists to this day—at an alarming scale. I posit this will only accelerate as we barrel toward the End Times.
Last week, someone made a comment in my presence that was said in jest, though somewhat antichurch. I reacted with silent offense at first, but I always try to respond as Jesus would—tempered, not hastily nor with contempt. As I pondered it over the day, I couldn’t help but agree with him. He did, in fact, have a point.
The church has a checkered history, and it should not be denied or covered up. This happens when the church tries to enter too far into the earthly realm, outside its directives from the Gospels: divine grace from Christ alone, spreading the message, helping the poor, and loving our neighbor. The Bible does not say to fleece people for more money, spread false teachings, or hold governments hostage. That is what happens when imperfect man enters the fray, spurred on by the demons and principalities that reign. The charge is simple: preach the true Gospel and let the Holy Spirit handle the details.
The doctrine of two kingdoms ultimately upholds another tenet of the faith: Thy will be done. The Lord’s work gets done through any means necessary, to use the parlance of our times—through you, through me, through governments, heathens, and the righteous alike. We are merely chess pieces being moved across the board.
When life gets really interesting, as I’ve said before, is when you start realizing your mission in life and begin embracing it. After all, are we not all heathens, at least on some level?
I’ll leave you with a Christmas quote to ponder from one of the greats: “A God whom we could understand would be no God.”
—Charles Spurgeon, Dec. 25, 1859
